The '''Wilson quotient''' ''W''(''p'') is defined as:

:<math>W(p) = \frac{(p-1)! + 1}{p}</math>

If ''p'' is a [[prime number]], the quotient is an [[integer]] by [[Wilson's theorem]]; moreover, if ''p'' is [[composite number|composite]], the quotient is not an integer. If ''p'' divides ''W''(''p''), it is called a [[Wilson prime]]. The integer values of ''W''(''p'') are {{OEIS|id=A007619}}:

: ''W''(2)&nbsp;=&thinsp;1
: ''W''(3)&nbsp;=&thinsp;1
: ''W''(5)&nbsp;=&nbsp;5
: ''W''(7)&nbsp;=&thinsp;103
: ''W''(11)&nbsp;=&nbsp;329891
: ''W''(13)&nbsp;=&nbsp;36846277
: ''W''(17)&nbsp;=&thinsp;1230752346353
: ''W''(19)&nbsp;=&nbsp;336967037143579
: ...

It is known that<ref name='Lehmer'>{{cite journal | last = Lehmer | first = Emma| title = On congruences involving Bernoulli numbers and the quotients of Fermat and Wilson| journal = Annals of Mathematics | year = 1938 | volume = 39 | issue = 2| pages = 350–360 | doi=10.2307/1968791| jstor = 1968791}}</ref>

:<math>W(p)\equiv B_{2(p-1)}-B_{p-1}\pmod{p},</math>
:<math>p-1+ptW(p)\equiv pB_{t(p-1)}\pmod{p^2},</math>
where <math>B_k</math> is the ''k''-th [[Bernoulli number]]. Note that the first relation comes from the second one by subtraction, after substituting <math>t=1</math> and <math>t=2</math>.
